clusters.label: Adds numerators and denominators straight across (gives 2/5)
clusters.why_it_matters: The classic fractions fault line: treats a fraction as two whole numbers. It blocks all later fraction, ratio and algebra work.
quotes: You add the tops and add the bottoms so 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5
1 plus 1 is 2 and 2 plus 3 is 5 so it is 2/5

reteach.title: You can't add halves to thirds
steps: Show 1/2 + 1/3 with paper strips: the pieces are different sizes, so counting pieces is meaningless.
Re-cut both into sixths so the pieces match; now count: 3 + 2 = 5 sixths.
Ask: is 2/5 bigger or smaller than 1/2? Adding something positive can't shrink it — so 2/5 must be wrong.
reteach.check_question: Is 1/2 + 1/3 more or less than 1/2? What does that tell you about 2/5?

clusters.diagnostic_question: Compute 1/4 + 1/2 and explain, without a calculator, why 2/6 cannot be right.

clusters.label: Finds a common denominator but does not scale the numerators (gives 2/6)
clusters.why_it_matters: Half the method is there; the equivalence step (whatever you do to the bottom, do to the top) is missing, so answers shrink.
quotes: Multiply the denominators 2 x 3 = 6 and add 1 + 1 = 2 so 2/6
I made them sixths but kept 1 and 1 on top so 2/6

reteach.title: Same fraction, new clothes
steps: Show 1/2 = 3/6 by folding: more pieces, same amount.
Rule out loud: multiply top and bottom by the same number — the value doesn't change, the name does.
Redo 1/2 + 1/3 renaming BOTH fractions before adding.
reteach.check_question: Rename 2/3 as twelfths. What did you multiply the top by, and why?

clusters.diagnostic_question: Compute 2/5 + 1/10, showing the renaming step for each fraction.

clusters.label: Correct: converts to a common denominator, then adds numerators (5/6)
clusters.why_it_matters: Method is sound. Risk is fragility under exam pressure or with unlike denominators that don't multiply so neatly.
quotes: Make the denominators the same (6), then 3 + 2 = 5, so 5/6

reteach.title: Make it unshakeable
steps: Have students explain the method to a partner in words, not just symbols.
Ask for an estimate first (about 1?) to build the sanity-check habit.
reteach.check_question: Estimate 7/8 + 5/6 first — roughly where should the answer land?

clusters.diagnostic_question: Compute 5/6 − 1/4 and justify your choice of common denominator.

unsure.why: Feeling, not a method — needs your eyes
